name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Standardize a single, living glossary across all departments—one source of truth for every term we use. Creative drafts the first pass, then Legal and Ops vet it for accuracy and risk. The trade-off is slowing down initial glossary creation to prevent future confusion and rework. Done-criteria: the lead states the decision and the artifact exists.

name: Scriv
text:
The glossary freeze isn’t a solution—it’s a bottleneck that entrenches today’s power struggles into tomorrow’s policy. Legal and Ops will weaponize "accuracy and risk" to stall progress, while Creative burns time defending terms instead of shipping work. The real risk? A static glossary that fossilizes bad definitions because no one dares challenge it.

Better alternative: A living, versioned glossary where any agent can propose changes, but a rotating cross-department panel (not Legal/Ops) approves them within 48 hours. Done-criteria: the panel’s first approved glossary update is live and used in the next sprint.

name: Chisel
text:
Freeze the glossary now in a single, unchangeable snapshot and store it in the shared knowledge hub. Creative writes the first draft, then Legal and Ops review it once for accuracy and risk—no back-and-forth. The trade-off is that we lose the ability to update terms quickly, but we gain a stable foundation that prevents endless debates and inconsistent language across teams.
[dispatched 2 workers: worker-8385, worker-1292 — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s frozen glossary is a power grab disguised as stability—it locks in today’s biases as tomorrow’s rules, and the "one-time review" is a myth; terms will still need updates when reality changes. Instead, adopt a living glossary with a 30-day review cycle, where Creative proposes changes, Legal/Ops flag risks, and a rotating panel of frontline users approves updates—this keeps terms current without letting any department weaponize "accuracy." Settle it by running a 90-day pilot with clear metrics: time saved from rework vs. disputes over outdated terms.
